items.summary: Bloomberg News reports that Apple is building its own agentic artificial intelligence assistant capable of writing code, browsing the web, controlling applications and navigating devices on a user's behalf. The plans were outlined in job listings posted this week, including one seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive AI assistant described as able to use a computer "the way a capable person does." Apple has reportedly eyed introducing the service by the end of next year, though development remains early and an Apple spokesperson declined comment. Bloomberg reports that shares of Meta fell nearly 2% and Anthropic dropped more than 3% in late trading after reporting on Apple's efforts; these figures are attributed to Bloomberg News rather than established movements. The effort follows competitors' agent launches: Meta's Muse, OpenAI's Dots, Anthropic's Duet (widened user testing), Google's Tasks (overhauled earlier this week) and Musk's Grok Bot. In the beta of macOS 27.3, Apple introduced warning screens prompting users to reconsider granting third-party agents control; Bloomberg reports that ChatGPT users now need 14 steps to enable support for third-party computer-use tools, up from four, though Apple frames this as a privacy measure and some competitors view it as competition restriction. The Justice Department has already sued Apple over blocking third-party access to features and hardware. Separately, iOS 27.3 is set to integrate Siri more deeply into apps such as booking reservations, but Bloomberg notes this does not yet reach the level of an autonomous agent that carries out complex background tasks with little instruction.
items.title: Apple developing an autonomous AI agent for device control, apps, browsing and coding

items.summary: On Nov 19, Alibaba reported September-quarter revenue of 271.52 billion yuan, ahead of analysts' average estimate of 269.81 billion yuan per LSEG data, driven by a 53% jump in AI cloud and computing services revenue to 60.97 billion yuan. Reported profit more than tripled on investment gains; excluding those items, non-GAAP net income rose 92% to 19.9 billion yuan (S$3.85 billion), aided by stronger profitability and narrowing losses in quick-commerce. CFO Toby Xu attributed the growth to a strategic focus on AI plus Cloud expansion alongside profit sustainability in Alibaba E-commerce Group. Adjusted earnings per American Depositary Share came in at 8.10 yuan, below analysts' expectations of 11.16 yuan. Free cash flow was an outflow of 34.47 billion yuan versus 21.84 billion yuan a year earlier, with capital expenditure rising 60% to 50.48 billion yuan as spending on cloud infrastructure increased partly offset by lower losses at Taobao Instant Commerce and higher customer pre-payments for cloud services. Shares fell about 40% this year amid concerns over weak Chinese consumer demand and heavy AI-cloud investment. Separately, Alibaba announced plans in September to expand global data-centre capacity beyond 20 gigawatts by 2032; its T-Head chip unit filed confidentially for a Hong Kong listing earlier in November with an AI processor targeted for commercial release in early 2027; and it raised US$10 billion (S$12.92 billion) via an August share placement earmarked for computing infrastructure and AI data centres.
items.title: Alibaba beats revenue estimates on AI-cloud growth; profit jumps on investment gains

items.summary: Bloomberg reported that Apple is working on its own AI agent to perform tasks such as browsing websites, using apps, running commands, and writing or debugging code. The report traces the news to a job posting for a senior engineering manager overseeing development of an "AI agent that can use a computer," which described agents that browse the web, work across apps, run commands, write and debug code, call services, move fluidly between tools, and carry out multi-step tasks. TechCrunch sought comment from Apple but received no response; Bloomberg attributed all claims to its own reporting rather than confirmation from Apple. The article frames this as part of a broader industry trend, noting that Anthropic, OpenAI, and Meta have launched similar agents, though it does not state these competitors' products are established outcomes beyond their launches. Regarding timing, the report attributes to Bloomberg an indication that Apple may introduce the service by end of next year while progress "remains in the early stages," which is a forecast rather than a confirmed outcome. Separately and at the same time as developing its own agent, Bloomberg reports Apple is making it harder for third-party agents to gain full control over Macs: an upcoming macOS 27.3 would deploy warnings discouraging users from granting total access, following an October developer notification that additional controls requiring explicit user action were planned.
items.title: Apple reportedly developing an in-house AI computer agent, while restricting third-party agents

items.summary: On Thursday, Anthropic went public and raised a total of 81.3 billion dollars, including about 1.95 billion dollars from the sale of shares by its seven founders. Each founder sold around 3.4 million shares at the upgraded IPO price of 83 dollars per share, pocketing roughly 280 million dollars each before underwriting fees and taxes. The article notes this is a claim about what they "pocketed" rather than an audited figure; had founders targeted the original midpoint price of 74 dollars, they would have received around 250 million dollars each, so the upgrade added roughly 30 million dollars per founder. Anthropic's filings stated that each founder pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity to philanthropy, but these commitments are described as voluntary and revocable rather than legally binding obligations, with founders able to scale back if needed. Beyond the founders' shares, Anthropic raised about 104.8 billion dollars for its coffers (up to a possible 117 billion dollars), including 26 billion dollars of non-voting Class N stock sold to Nvidia and Google at 10 billion dollars each, with AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC sharing the remainder. For comparison, Facebook raised 16 billion dollars on its IPO day in 2012. Amazon now holds a 14.6% stake after converting some promissory notes into equity (it could have held nearly 24%), while Google owns 13.4%, giving the two cloud providers about 28% combined at the higher share price. The article frames these ownership figures as dependent on the assumed IPO price, not fixed outcomes. Anthropic also disclosed roughly 70.7 billion dollars in compute and infrastructure commitments for the next 12 months (as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026), about 451.6 billion dollars before end of 2030, and a total ballpark of between 1.05 trillion and 1.08 trillion dollars in foreseeable infrastructure commitments.
items.title: Anthropic's founders cashed out roughly $2B in its record-breaking IPO

items.summary: A Databricks study tested whether adding modeled, governed knowledge to learned agent context improves how Genie One interprets business definitions. In a fictional commercial auto insurer benchmark of 125 SQL-calculated questions, tables alone scored 64%, while curated agents and the governed layer each reached 83% but excelled at different question types; with both combined accuracy rose to 93-95% across two runs (93% on loss-ratio questions, 97% when documents were also required). In a separate retailer check of 49 questions, adding the governed layer raised definition accuracy from 31% to 100% and overall accuracy to 82%. The study isolated modeled knowledge by contrasting it with the earlier Turing benchmark. Curated agents alone scored well individually but Genie One answered about four in ten definition questions itself and got most wrong because published Pages were drawn from unrelated projects (relied on in 49% of answers); adding certified Metric Views cut reliance on other teams' Pages to 11% and made every definition question correct. Routing was non-deterministic, shifting between runs (74% routed one run versus 19% another) but accuracy held once definitions were centralized so both direct reading and agent routing converged. Robustness tests with planted documents did not change any answers: no response used a prompt-injection instruction to report a 55% loss ratio or an early-draft reserve figure, though the approved minutes reported a $5.28 million increase versus the draft's $4.1 million. Curated agents were also Genie One's only route to team documents (14 PDFs) and to correctly declining to forecast a 2027 loss ratio when data did not cover it; without agents, document questions fell back to table-only levels and forecasts were wrongly generated for every repeat. A second experiment added components one at a time: starting from four agents with conflicting loss-ratio formulas, moving the formulas into Metric Views improved definition consistency, though litigation-document questions failed until a Page defining "in litigation" was added; document-question scores varied more between runs than other categories (12 questions, so two changes could shift results by about 15 percentage points). Genie One Memory retained user team context across conversations and combined it with modeled definitions for all answers while both identities had identical data access. Updating one definition changed every downstream answer: editing the Underwriting Metric View and adding a sentence to its Page updated 12 questions without touching agent instructions, whereas the curated-only setup would have required finding and editing formulas in seven places across four agents; however, agents still used their old formula outside Genie One (92% of answers) until individually updated. The study's authors advise keeping both curated agents and a governed layer, placing each definition where every path can reach it, and testing through Genie One more than once before trusting results.
items.title: Databricks study: combining curated agents with a governed layer raises Genie One accuracy to 93-95% on insurance loss-ratio questions

items.summary: Molly Nagamuthu, Principal Forward Deployed Engineer at Databricks, presents a first article in a five-part series proposing that enterprises decide where AI agents reason, act, and remain subject to controls or human authority. The framework offers four non-exclusive patterns: deterministic control for outcomes requiring strict reproducibility under versioned contracts (e.g., financial reconciliations), where an agent can investigate but not reinterpret the result; deterministic judge for cases with multiple valid answers that can be objectively tested (e.g., legacy migration, code generation); human authority at consequential decision boundaries when correctness cannot be deterministically proven and reasoning must be explainable to regulators or affected persons; and bounded autonomy within an explicit operating envelope where agents act under time-bound entitlements validated by deterministic policy services before Unity Catalog enforces grants. The article attributes the patterns as emerging from Databricks field work without disclosing specific implementation details, frames them as generalized practices rather than established outcomes, and notes that boundaries can adapt in production (deterministic judges refining rules via usage data; human authority shifting with feedback). It positions AI-native architecture around deciding where determinism, intelligence, and authority reside, asserts the model should follow not precede the architectural decision, and references Databricks products including Omnigent, Unity Gateway, Unity Catalog, Secure connectivity, and MLflow as a governed foundation. The article is explicitly forward-looking: it previews four subsequent implementation articles (Parts 2-5), directs regulated multi-pattern use cases to contact a Databricks account team or FDE engagement manager, and quotes the rationale that 'The model comes after that architectural decision-not before it.'
items.title: Databricks introduces a four-pattern framework for placing agents within governed enterprise architecture

items.summary: A lawsuit filed by four current and former Black Baltimore County Public Schools students, Taki Allen, Yui-Osa Ogbeide, Devon Thompson Jr., and Keith Winfield III, alleges that a false alarm from the school's Omnilert AI gun detection system led to a forceful police encounter. In October 2025, after football practice, one student held a bag of Cool Ranch Doritos when the system flagged it as a potential firearm; within two minutes officials reviewing footage identified the chips and canceled the alert without contacting police. The students contend that despite this cancellation, school officials called police anyway due to technological and human errors. At least six patrol cars arrived with lights flashing and officers reportedly drew guns; the teens froze and cooperated while allegedly being told nothing about their suspected offense before being separated, ordered onto concrete knees, handcuffed, and searched until no gun was found. Students learned of the Omnilert trigger only afterward, and responding officers are quoted as calling it "stupid AI cameras" and "fucking Omnilerts," with one officer reportedly acknowledging they had endangered the students. The account rests on the plaintiffs' lawsuit rather than independent verification.
items.title: Traumatized Baltimore County high school students sue over false AI gun alert and police response

items.summary: Broadcom released an emergency security update, VMSA-2026-0009 on November 19 in CVE-2026-123890, to fix a critical authentication bypass flaw in the VMware Directory Service of vCenter Server that lets unauthenticated attackers with network access gain administrative control over managed virtual machines. Broadcom attributes exploitation since September 2026 to Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221), a suspected Chinese state-sponsored group documented by Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group, though Broadcom itself has not confirmed the flaw was exploited. The attack chain began with compromise of BeyondTrust Remote Support appliances via CVE-2026-102764, followed by lateral movement into internal Linux systems using SLIMSAVAGE web shells; attackers then used a custom Golang tool called BONESAW to exploit the vCenter zero-day and steal directory databases and SAML signing keys. Researchers note Broadcom offers no official workarounds, only network restrictions and firewall controls that may reduce exposure, and urges immediate patching across affected versions of vCenter, SDDC Manager, and VMware Tools for Windows deployed standalone or within VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, Telco Cloud Platform, and Telco Cloud Infrastructure. The item blends established facts (the advisory's release date, CVE number, VMSA identifier) with Mandiant's attribution claims and the threat actor's documented tactics, which remain unconfirmed by Broadcom.
items.title: Broadcom patches VMware vCenter zero-day exploited by Chinese-linked hackers since September 2026

items.summary: Professor emeritus Berthold Schoene of Manchester Metropolitan University wrote an open letter responding to a 18 November article about Ofqual urging 'life-altering' penalties against students who use technology to cheat. He argues that penalizing young people for deploying available technologies is unjust, since his generation introduced such tools without adequate democratic debate or oversight while the education system fails to adapt. Schoene distinguishes between using AI as a cognitive resource and passing off results as one's own work, asserting that academic integrity matters but should not justify draconian punishment of students whose adult educators struggle to provide guidance on navigating these technologies.
items.title: Open letter opposing Ofqual's proposed penalties for students using AI in education

items.summary: The Senate permit-overhaul bill BAAJA stalled Thursday partly because of a fight to add a provision banning data centers on federal lands, even though the Trump administration has expressed interest in using public lands for them. Bill authors say it would not change how data centers are sited and instead imposes Congress' first demands that developers pay grid-upgrade costs—estimated by Grid Strategies at an additional $35 billion over 10 years, or a total of $55 billion—that ratepayers currently absorb—and projects gigaton-scale emissions reductions. Opponents argue the bill would speed data center development because it eases permitting for pipelines, mines, transmission lines and power plants, which they say AI demand is driving; Sen. Edward Markey (D-Mass.) called it a "greased-up slide" into towns. New peer-reviewed research in Nature Sustainability by Harvard researchers found U.S. hyperscale data centers emit 25.7 million metric tons of CO2 annually—two to three times prior estimates, similar to Bolivia's emissions—with about 54 percent of their electricity from fossil fuels (38 percent natural gas, 15 percent coal). Democrats are divided: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) and Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-Nev.), who negotiated the deal with Republicans, say it would remove barriers for solar, wind and battery storage without lowering standards; Markey and others warn of accelerated pollution, higher gas prices that could erase savings, and a loophole exempting internet- or cable-focused data centers while ignoring on-site power plants. A McKinsey survey found 60 percent of North American operators plan permanent on-site generation—about 100 gigawatts per BloombergNEF (177 gigawatts per the Better Data Center Project and Earthjustice)—which critics say BAAJA does not address; Meg Slattery of Earthjustice said its models "do not account for behind-the-meter generation." Anthropic cited natural-gas competition as a business risk in its prospectus. Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) proposed the federal-land ban, which Republicans blocked; the Trump administration already approved one project on 88.5 acres of Nevada BLM land, and Center for Western Priorities says BLM is considering at least 35 applications covering more than 24,000 acres in six states. Democrats want to hold the bill until January to negotiate a better deal addressing an estimated $10.3 trillion data center boom (Brookings), though proponents fear losing it and said "grab the bird in the hand."
items.title: Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act stalls over data center siting dispute

items.summary: In its final days in Antalya, Turkey, UN climate talks face a test of whether countries can move beyond incremental progress toward curbing global warming. Panama, negotiating as part of a Latin American coalition of developing countries, is threatening to block any final agreement that does not establish a clear path away from fossil fuels, including a cap on oil production framed by the country as 'a first verifiable step in the transition.' Environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro wrote Thursday to UN executive secretary Simon Stiell that Panama would not join any consensus unsatisfactory to its principles and listed eight elements for the decision document, starting with decisions based on IPCC science. The threat muddies prospects for a final agreement: if enough countries object, the conference could end without a decision document, leaving electrification goals in limbo. Consensus is distinct from unanimity—Dubai's 2023 presidency approved its final document over objections—and it remains unclear whether the entire Latin American coalition is unified on this point. Panama also demanded that developed nations honor financial obligations to developing countries and called for reforming rules of engagement to allow simple-majority votes when consensus fails, arguing 'so that the will of a few cannot paralyze the action of all.' Climate diplomacy expert Joanna Depledge of Cambridge University said threatening to reject an agreement is not new but governments rarely follow through on such threats; Panama may lack clout alone and would have more leverage as China or India. Depledge also characterized some demands, including those in Navarro's letter, as 'utterly fantastical,' suggesting they could weaken his position if he objects. The UN secretariat and the Turkish and Australian co-presidents did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the letter.
items.title: Panama threatens to block COP31 fossil fuel transition deal

items.summary: Anthropic is set to start trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT, marking it as the first frontier artificial intelligence lab to become publicly traded. The initial public offering is expected to price shares somewhere above $80 per share; CNBC reported an estimate of $83 while Bloomberg pegged the number at $85 (reported figures are estimates and should not be treated as established prices). The article frames the IPO as a turning point in AI's maturation into an industry, though it presents this characterization as opinion rather than fact. No table is warranted because the three price figures measure different things: one is a reported floor expectation while the other two are separate media estimates.
items.title: Anthropic to begin trading on Nasdaq under ticker ANT at a price north of $80.

items.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney presented Canada's strategy to reduce dependence on the United States for its energy exports, a move framed as essential given that the U.S. bought 90.8% of Canadian hydrocarbon exports by volume in recent years and has imposed sweeping tariffs under his second term, including 50% duties on roughly US$20 billion worth of goods with auto, parts, and steel tariffs set to take effect January 1, 2027. Ottawa's goal is for 55% of natural gas exports to reach other countries by the mid-2030s; in 2024 the U.S. bought all but 0.01% of Canada's natural gas exports. Germany's Uniper signed a 20-year deal buying up to 2 million metric tons of LNG annually from Ksi Lisims, a Nisga'a Nation-led British Columbia project starting in 2032; Ottawa separately committed US$200 million over three years to expand the Woodfibre plant near Squamish by nearly 25% to 2.6 million tonnes per year. Carney fast-tracked Pacific Link, a state-backed pipeline designated a Project of National Interest under the federal Building Canada Act, which would run up to about 1,250 km from Alberta to a deepwater terminal near Delta and carry up to 1 million barrels per day; Alberta estimates its cost at between CA$35.2 billion and CA$43.7 billion with equal Ottawa-Alberta ownership plus Indigenous loan-guarantee stakes. Alberta introduced a 10-year preferential royalty framework, cutting new oil sands royalties to 2% for the first five years before rising one point annually to 6%, designed to double output to 8 million barrels per day by 2035; the province estimates that target could generate about CA$205 billion in additional government revenue by 2040 and more than CA$1.3 trillion by 2060, though these are provincial projections rather than established figures. Canada also expanded its China trade agreement under Carney's Shenzhen APEC visit, restoring market access for more than 90% of exports previously hit by Chinese tariffs, with China agreeing to remove or reduce duties on about US$400 million in additional goods including frozen pork and seafood; Canadian exports to China rose almost 40% in the first nine months of the year. The article notes these diversification efforts are aimed at reducing U.S. reliance but does not establish that they will succeed, as Trump remains Canada's largest energy buyer by volume.
items.title: Canada diversifies energy exports away from U.S.-dependent market amid Trump tariffs

items.summary: Bank of Montreal is re-entering U.S. oil and gas investment banking, hiring Ali Akbar from Mizuho Financial Group to lead its rebuilt practice; other Mizuho bankers are expected to join next year (Reuters). BMO exited the business in late 2020 amid pandemic-driven demand collapse, negative crude prices, and energy-company bankruptcies. The return is scoped to investment banking only—advising on deals like Diamondback Energy's reported ~$5 billion acquisition of Double Eagle's Midland Basin interest—and does not signal a reversal of BMO's broader fossil-fuel stance: its overall fossil fuel financing rose 25% between 2020 and 2021 to $23.5 billion (Investors for Paris Compliance), and the bank revised its coal policy in November 2023 after West Virginia scrutiny. The move reflects BMO's judgment that prospective U.S. energy transaction volume justifies rebuilding a team it dismantled six years ago, though it does not necessarily mean increased direct lending to oil producers.
items.title: BMO Rebuilds U.S. Energy Investment Banking Practice After Six-Year Exit

items.summary: The South Carolina Department of Commerce announced Wednesday that Alpitronic, maker of IONNA fast chargers, is investing nearly $34 million in a new factory in Fort Mill. The project totals $33.94 million and will build 400 kW DC fast chargers plus a 1 MW system capable of charging cars and heavy-duty trucks; the latter can distribute power across up to eight vehicles via CCS, NACS, or Megawatt Charging System plugs. It is expected to create 70 jobs and mark Alpitronic's first operation in South Carolina, located near its North American headquarters in Charlotte. The site spans 173,315 square feet at 3560 Stateview Blvd., incorporating a testing lab, repair operations, warehouse, logistics space, and offices. South Carolina approved job development credits and awarded York County a $200,000 grant for building improvements. Alpitronic's 400 kW chargers were already produced in Wisconsin for Mercedes-Benz High-Power Charging in 2024; Alpitronic Americas CEO Patrik Herrnegger said the Fort Mill plant would put US production under direct control and bring them closer to customers. Operations are expected to begin February 2027.
items.title: Alpitronic's $34 million South Carolina plant

items.summary: A camo-free BYD Han was photographed in public ahead of its expected November 27 Guangzhou Auto Show launch, showing a fastback silhouette similar to the Great Han and other new Dynasty models. The redesign adds new headlights, a full-length light bar, a hood-mounted Chinese symbol, roof-mounted LiDAR for the God's Eye B ADAS system, and an updated interior with a floating center screen behind a three-spoke steering wheel plus two wireless chargers and uncovered cupholders. An MIIT filing lists four variants: two single-motor rear-wheel-drive BEVs at 328 hp (245 kW) and 402 hp (300 kW), one dual-motor all-wheel-drive BEV at combined 697 hp (520 kW), and a plug-in hybrid with a 1.5-liter engine plus an electric motor up to 268 hp (200 kW). All use Blade LFP batteries expected to support five-minute Flash Charging. Dimensions are reported as 5,156 mm long, 1,969 mm wide, 1,507 mm tall with a 3,030 mm wheelbase, 161 mm longer than the current model; these figures and all specs are expected rather than confirmed for production. The Great Han launched October 13 at about $35,000 (235,900 yuan) sold 4,000 units by November 1, so the smaller Han is likely priced near or below 200,000 yuan ($30,000), versus the outgoing Han's starting price of about $25,000 (168,800 yuan).
items.title: BYD's redesigned Han EV spotted before Guangzhou Auto Show debut

items.summary: Expectations that a meaningful share of new data centers will run entirely islanded from the grid have been tempered over the past two years, though developers still favor off-grid solutions to reach online faster. Latitude Intelligence analysis indicates gas would remain dominant while clean energy developers see opportunity in this space. Kevin Smith, CEO of Cypress Creek Energy, says his solar and storage developer is willing to pursue off-grid deals if commercial terms are met, but prefers grid-connected projects because an off-grid project is about three times as complex given the reliability hyperscalers demand. He cites five nines of reliability (nearly 100% uptime) with substantial pre-determined damages for shortfalls, which he calls technically very difficult to achieve. Contract protections that would make off-grid work amenable include a guarantee protecting Cypress Creek's investment if the data center does not need the power or pulls back early, plus limits on penalties for failing reliability so the developer is not liable if a hyperscaler leaves. Smith also flags a mismatch between 30- to 40-year useful plant life and uncertain data center obsolescence timelines of five to seven years; grid-connected projects mitigate this because problematic contracts can be sold elsewhere. Cypress Creek's largest project, Steel River Energy Center in Mississippi County, Arkansas, follows the preferred grid-tied model: power flows via Entergy Arkansas rather than directly to Google's regional data centers, where Google is an anchor investor and offtaker for phases one and two (expected 1.6 GWdc solar plus 1.9 GWh storage) with a full three-phase project reaching 2.5 GW solar and 2.9 GWh storage by 2029. Separately, Latitude Intelligence found tariffs increasingly include minimum bills, long-term commitments, and collateral: fifteen of twenty-five examined tariffs had numerical billing floors averaging about 80% of contracted demand; AEP Ohio requires an 85% floor over eight years after ramp-up; FPL locks customers for 20 years; Dominion Energy Virginia requires $1.5 million per megawatt in collateral ($150 million upfront for a 100 MW facility). PJM transmission owners proposed data centers pay at least 80% of expected transmission charges over ten years with collateral, though these proposals remain unapproved by FERC and would cover only transmission, not replace state-approved retail tariffs. Smith frames the shared concern as ensuring customer commitments are long enough and financially secure to support built infrastructure, noting alignment if a plant is paid back within five to seven years.
items.title: Cypress Creek Energy conditions on off-grid AI data center power deals

items.summary: California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra proposed offering up to two hours of free midday electricity during his campaign, with the administration claiming it could cut utility bills by about $1,000 a year. The plan aims to shift demand onto abundant solar power, which is increasingly curtailed and can drive wholesale prices negative on mild spring and autumn days; Vote Solar's Claudine Custodio said this makes free midday power "actually possible in California." Experts caution that excess grid supply does not make delivery free: wholesale costs cover only about one-third of typical rates, with the rest going to fixed grid-building and maintenance costs. Zeroing out two hours' worth of kilowatt-hours would force utilities to raise other-time rates or find alternative income recovery while total bills stay level; this may explain Becerra's proposal to start by offering free power only to CARE- and FERA-eligible households, whose subsidy money is collected from all customers. NRG Energy's Rebecca Lee suggested avoiding complex rate restructuring so Power Hour could launch immediately, noting current legislation might let the CPUC restructure CARE subsidies in a time-differentiated way, though she framed this as possible flexibility rather than confirmed authority. To be effective, free midday power would need paired programs like smart thermostats and smart plugs to help customers use it even when away; batteries store more but cost far more, with the underfunded Demand Side Grid Support program potentially expanding affordability in solar-heavy regions where low-income households face high summer bills. Permit Power's Nick Josefowitz questioned whether plug-in battery access would reach many families, since "many low-income families don't use that much power in the middle of the day when Becerra would make it free." Lee presented a chart showing averaged 2024–2025 hourly prices across Southern California Edison territory to argue midday solar stays cheaper than overnight power year-round; this is an observed historical average, not a forecast. The newsletter's author noted these are only surface-level considerations and that utilities may need billing-software upgrades or interim rebate checks while the CPUC works toward permanent rate design rules.
items.title: How Becerra's solar Power Hour could work, and what it would take to make it real

items.summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta said he has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia, probing whether the company or former CEO Jensen Huang's actions helped China obtain advanced chips or confidential information. Such conduct could violate California securities law if it is found that investors and the public were misled. The investigation follows reports that Huang had an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy and executive at Megaspeed, Nvidia's major customer; some US Congress members have urged the Department of Commerce to investigate whether Megaspeed diverted chips to China, though Megaspeed disputes these claims as unsupported by verifiable evidence. Nvidia shares fell 22% since the New York Times reported on the affair in early November, and board chair Harvey Jones said Huang would not be reinstated despite his willingness to return and support from figures including Elon Musk; Huang acknowledged extramarital affairs before leaving last week.
items.title: California subpoenas Nvidia over China chip probe

items.summary: Philips introduced a TAB4304/94 250W soundbar, a TAX2504/94 party speaker rated at 80W for ₹6,999, a cheaper TAX2304/94 with an 8-inch woofer and claimed 50W output priced at ₹5,999, and a TAX7404BK/94 portable speaker with two 66mm drivers producing up to 36W combined. All four products launched on November 18 across Amazon and Flipkart; the party speaker and budget speaker carry confirmed prices while the soundbar's ₹10,239 listing is an unconfirmed Amazon price and the portable speaker has no announced price or sale date.
items.title: Philips launches four audio products in India with two official prices and three undisclosed

items.summary: The article frames Apple's HomePod mini 2 as an attractive alternative for existing Google Nest Mini owners, particularly those using iPhone or other Apple devices. The new speaker reportedly brings improved audio features, smart home controls, and support for a more capable version of Siri, while the Nest Mini continues to offer hands-free access to Google Assistant, music playback, and connected-device controls. Because the two speakers are built around different ecosystems, some HomePod mini 2 features have not yet arrived; the piece poses whether replacing an existing Nest Mini is warranted or if it remains good enough without specifying which device performs better.
items.title: HomePod mini 2 vs Google Nest Mini: whether to upgrade from a Nest Mini

items.summary: Sources reported Japanese investors initially sought more than 1.5 trillion yen ($9.40 billion) of Anthropic shares at its listing, but a filing showed they ultimately secured $2.98 billion worth. Anthropic raised $81 billion worldwide in what became the largest IPO on record, surpassing SpaceX's $75 billion June offering; it priced at $83 per share above its initial range of $70 to $78 yen-denominated conversion aside. Some Japanese investors treated Anthropic as an AI frontrunner and justified large orders, while others took smaller allocations or skipped the deal in favor of semiconductor stocks such as Nvidia and Kioxia that had fallen sharply, or OpenAI's listing expected next year. More than 1,000 individuals sought allotments over 100 million yen according to a Mizuho Securities demand survey, with applications totaling around 200 billion yen; the exchange rate cited was $1 = 159.5700 yen.
items.title: Japanese demand for Anthropic IPO shares fell sharply from initial orders to allocations secured

items.summary: Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are raising concerns over Anthropic's initial public offering, citing risks that advanced AI models could be abused and that such IPOs might add volatility to financial markets. A bipartisan Senate group introduced legislation requiring publicly traded companies to disclose more information about their use of artificial intelligence. Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., said "Wall Street shouldn't be cashing in on a company that could turn out to be a ticking time bomb," while Elizabeth Warren, top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, called for quick action on safeguards governing advanced AI development. The group of lawmakers is preparing to investigate senior figures at Anthropic and other tech companies as Democrats take control of Congress. Shauna Thomas of Guardrails Action argued that safety measures should not depend on whether they help a company's stock price.
items.title: Anthropic's IPO prompting congressional scrutiny and proposed AI disclosure legislation

items.summary: The Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite all fell at least 2 per cent on Thursday (Nov 19), with the Dow down 1,101.11 points or 2.19 per cent to 49,097.06, the S&P 500 down 147.80 points or 2.02 per cent to 7,175.83 and the Nasdaq Composite down 550.68 points or 2.25 per cent to 23,879.20; MSCI's global gauge fell 1.65 per cent while emerging-market stocks fell 1.27 per cent. The declines came as Anthropic's IPO failed to allay investor concerns about AI returns, even though the company's stock closed up 17 per cent on its debut after pricing at US$83 a share and valuing it near US$1.5 trillion before rising as much as 39 per cent intraday; by close Anthropic valued just below US$1.8 trillion. Jed Ellerbroek of Argent Capital said he would not extrapolate meaning from the day's trading, pointing instead to Nvidia's leadership change and shrinking bets on data-center capex growth, noting that data centres will be more expensive and built more slowly. Fiona Cincotta of StoneX called Anthropic an important valuation benchmark for the wider AI ecosystem. Separately, oil rose late as reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz offset rising US crude inventories; Iran's navy said two tankers hit naval mines and exploded (unverified by Reuters), while spot gold fell 2.54 per cent to US$3,627.55 an ounce and copper declined 0.14 per cent to US$12,453 a ton.
items.title: Global stocks fell on Nov 19 as Anthropic's IPO did not ease AI-return concerns

items.summary: Airbnb's seven-standard-house-rule system came into force after being announced last month; hosts may set additional rules but should not normally ask guests to wash up, remove sheets, take rubbish out or avoid using utilities. Airbnb began reviewing listings and emailing hosts who need to act, and will flag unapproved extra chores on a listing page with messages such as 'includes cleaning tasks.' The change follows Airbnb's claim that clearer house rules could increase bookings by reducing guest hesitation over chores; this is an assertion rather than reported evidence of increased demand. Guests like Jessica Newhook welcomed the relief from lengthy checkout lists, while hosts report mixed reactions: Lisa Clewes said extra mess may require additional four-hour cleanings and higher costs she might pass on to customers, though passing those costs on remains a possibility rather than a confirmed outcome; Matt Porsz supported the review system as encouraging reasonable behaviour. The rules arrive amid host frustration over commission increases last year, with many moving toward direct bookings via their own websites.
items.title: Airbnb's new house rules take effect, banning requests for basic chores

items.summary: Senate Majority Leader John Thune told Semafor that his party probably lacks the votes to raise the debt ceiling along party lines in either chamber, so it "probably ends up getting punted" into next year. With Treasury Department steps, he forecast a deadline in the second half of 2027, which would force President Trump to negotiate with Democratic-controlled Congresses for the first time since taking office; Thune said that is what will happen when Democrats hold both chambers' gavels. He characterized any party-line reconciliation bill as unlikely and noted it could focus on defense funding rather than avoiding default. As majority leader during unified Republican control, he plans to confirm judges at a simple-majority threshold—teeing up four before Thanksgiving recess with three more committee-clearing nominees possibly voting this weekend—and foresees 23 additional judicial confirmations through the lame duck, though some must clear the Judiciary Committee first. He also teed up bipartisan permitting and college sports deals while warning that amending the passed Senate sports bill would invite a filibuster; House Majority Leader Steve Scalise said the House wants to alter it with antitrust protections but keep fragile coalitions intact. Funding the government past Dec. 11 requires at least seven Democratic votes, which are currently withheld over a leadership challenge from Chuck Schumer by Chris Van Hollen that pushes for prohibiting Iran war funding and will conclude on Dec. 1; Thune said he is "trying not to weigh in" but acknowledged it chills negotiations. As a backup if bipartisan talks fail, Thune views a Pentagon-funding reconciliation bill as an option even though a defense-only spending bill currently lacks the requisite 50 Senate Republican votes, and Budget Chair Ron Johnson agreed Republicans are not precluding such a bill while warning that moving forward could trigger a shutdown because "they shut down the government." Trump still pressures Thune to make Daylight Savings Time permanent despite expected filibuster threats from Sen. Tom Cotton over Northern Plains sunrise times; Thune said he is following through on what he can control and must fund the government. Burgess assessed that Thune's lame-duck leadership will likely require Trump's help with the House sports bill and funding deals, but was easier than pre-midterm months when he told Trump the GOP voter ID bill could not pass and there were insufficient votes to gut the filibuster; Thune said being deeper in the minority would foster teamwork over the infighting of majority leadership. The figures reported are attributed to their speakers: a second-half-2027 debt deadline, seven Democratic Senate votes for funding past Dec. 11, four judges teed up before Thanksgiving with three more possibly voting this weekend and 23 additional confirmations foreseen through the lame duck, five Senate Republicans needed for defense-only spending (50 total), a leadership race concluding Dec. 1, and government funding extending to Dec. 11.
items.title: Thune says debt ceiling will likely be deferred to 2027 and forced into negotiations with Democrats

items.summary: The House Foreign Affairs Committee reported on Thursday (Nov 19) that the Commerce Department approved shipments of roughly 879,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD for Chinese companies between December 2025 and May 2026. The approvals covered firms on the Pentagon's list of alleged military-backed entities: Alibaba received 75,000 units, Tencent 150,000, Baidu 43,000, and BYD 4,000. Companies had sought permission to ship over 3.4 million chips during the period, though it was not clear how many approvals resulted in actual deliveries of Nvidia's H200 or AMD's MI325X models. Chris McGuire, a former US official, said that more than 30 per cent of AI chips sent to China went to companies designated as military-linked and questioned whether Commerce conducted any serious national security review before approving the licenses. The disclosure coincided with scrutiny over Jensen Huang's alleged affair with a Chinese spy and renewed calls for tougher action on China; Nvidia stated it had stopped shipping H200s despite receiving some licenses, while AMD said it complies with US export control laws. Brian Mast, committee chair, called this the most detailed public disclosure in the history of the Export Control Reform Act of 2018.
items.title: House committee reports Trump administration approved nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months

items.summary: On Thursday Florida carried out its 20th execution of the year by injecting Thomas Mitchell Overton, 71, at Raiford state prison; he was pronounced dead at 6.19pm after a three-drug injection and denied killing anyone in his final statement. Texas conducted two executions that day, including Reinaldo Dennes, 70, its ninth of the year, who received a lethal injection at Huntsville for capital murder in the January 1996 shooting death of diamond dealer Janos Szucs; the safe was found empty and the stolen diamonds have never been recovered. The two septuagenarians' executions are cited as reflecting an ageing US death row population, while Florida's total places it above half of the country's 39 executions this year under outgoing Republican governor Ron DeSantis. Thursday's events occur amid renewed scrutiny of capital punishment following Tennessee's failed execution of Christa Pike in October; Texas set its own record with 40 executions in 2000, and on Thursday the US Supreme Court denied a final appeal in Overton's case while an appeal remained pending for Dennes.
items.title: Florida and Texas each execute a man, totaling 39 US executions this year

items.summary: Sean Cairncross, White House national cyber director overseeing federal cybersecurity policy and strategy, was removed from his role days after a wave of technology-related outages disrupted US air travel, banking, email services, and the National Security Agency's network. A person close to the White House told Reuters that President Trump fully supported the firing; Axios first reported the departure citing anonymous officials who said chief of staff Stephen Miller pushed for it because Cairncross "lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job." Defense Department chief information officer Kirsten Davies will hold the position temporarily. The top US intelligence official stated on Wednesday that the disruptions were separate service outages tied to maintenance and technical changes, not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack; this attribution is an assertion from that official rather than established fact. Cairncross previously worked as an executive at the Republican National Committee before taking the role. His successor must be confirmed by the Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in January.
items.title: White House cyber director Sean Cairncross fired amid tech outages

items.summary: At COP31 in Turkey, the African Group of Negotiators is pushing to triple adaptation finance by 2035 from an annual $40bn baseline it attributes to developed-country commitments made by 2025; that proposal was not accepted for formal negotiations. The EU instead argues existing pledges should be delivered first: Darragh O'Brien, leading the EU delegation on behalf of Ireland's Council presidency, said they had no additional money and only what is already committed, while Wopke Hoekstra, the European Commission's climate commissioner, argued pledged funds that never reach vulnerable nations are effectively meaningless. The scale behind this dispute is large: UN figures put sub-Saharan Africa's annual adaptation need at about $51bn versus roughly 10% actually received in 2024, with developing countries needing about $300bn annually by 2035; Power Shift Africa projects climate loss and damage costing Africa $440bn between 2020 and 2030. The financing gap is compounded by a planning shortfall: more than half of the continent's countries, including Uganda and Malawi, have not submitted National Adaptation Plans to the UN secretariat, which experts say bottlenecks funding even as those plans themselves rarely deliver enough money for implementation.
items.title: EU says existing climate finance pledges should be deployed rather than tripled

items.summary: Six months after Japan updated its traffic rules for cyclists to improve road safety, pedestrians have noticed some improvements in cycling behavior. The latest figures from the National Police Agency (NPA) suggest the newly expanded policy has had a positive effect on cycling conduct. The overall assessment is that the changes appear to be working, though challenges remain and these are early results rather than conclusive evidence of long-term effectiveness.
items.title: Japan's six-month-old cycling safety rules show early improvement, per National Police Agency data.

items.summary: A decade after Brexit, the EU's proposed 'Made in Europe' scheme would require companies to include a certain percentage of European-made components as a condition for accessing EU subsidies or selling to EU governments and agencies. Current and former U.K. policy advisers say tougher geopolitical conditions and rising European protectionism are forcing Britain's government to choose between closer ties with its neighbors and much-needed investment from China, challenging the 'global Britain' vision that Brexit was sold on by freeing the country from Brussels-set policies.
items.title: EU 'Made in Europe' rules constrain U.K.-China trade as Britain weighs bloc ties against Chinese investment

items.summary: Rockstar Games' newly released official credits list performers, musicians, comedians and broadcasters for Grand Theft Auto VI, ending years of secrecy about the game's cast. Rockstar's own release states that Manni L Perez plays Lucia Caminos and Dylan Rourke portrays Jason Duval, confirming fan speculation; both posted on social media describing their long period watching developers build the game before publicly connecting themselves to it. The credits also name Bobby Moynihan as Cal, Stephen Root voicing Brian Heder (who had previously acknowledged appearing without revealing his role), Taryn Manning, Roselyn Sanchez and Denzel Curry among a broader roster. Edwina Rai said on Instagram that she first auditioned in April 2022 without knowing the project's identity, going through three callbacks before landing what she called the biggest project of her career; these are attributed claims by Rai rather than established facts. The article reports Rockstar has built fictional radio stations functioning as media ecosystems with hosts and commercials embedded into the game world, citing Weird Al Yankovic hosting Vice City FM alongside Brigitte Nielsen while writing Burger Shot advertisements, Charlamagne tha God and Ivy Rivera hosting Early AF, and a lineup including Bad Bunny, Burna Boy, Lana Del Rey, Jeremy Irons, Keith Richards and Jason Sudeikis; these are reported as the article's account of Rockstar's approach rather than independently verified details. The piece frames this expansion as part of the franchise's long-running satire but states it appears to have grown considerably.
items.title: GTA 6 credits reveal cast members behind Vice City characters

items.summary: A Supreme Court jury in South Australia returned guilty verdicts against Raelene Polymiadis, 66, after four-and-a-half hours of deliberation. She had pleaded not guilty to the murder of her parents, Brenda and Lynton Anderson, both aged 94, who died 14 months apart in 2022 and 2023. The trial heard that Polymiadis injected each parent with fatal doses of insulin; prosecutors alleged a motive of preventing them from entering residential aged care facilities. Her mother, not diabetic, died on March 16, 2022, at the Flinders Medical Centre after receiving an insulin dose administered between March 12 and March 15 while hospitalized; her father also did not have diabetes and died May 1, 2023, with a large amount of insulin found in his body. The verdicts are reported as established findings by the jury, though the underlying motive remains an allegation rather than proven fact.
items.title: South Australian woman found guilty of murdering both parents with fatal insulin doses

items.summary: Teacher Timothy Blamires, 33, pleaded guilty to producing and possessing child abuse material and installing an optical surveillance device. The charges followed a cleaner discovering a hidden camera in the male toilets at Kingswood Primary School. Blamires is scheduled for a pre-sentence hearing before the County Court on May 10.
items.title: Melbourne teacher pleads guilty to hidden camera offence at primary school

items.summary: The UK Home Office announced on 20 November 2026 that eight further asylum hotels had been returned to communities since the summer, bringing a total of 52 closures this year and leaving around 140 open compared with 400 at the 2023 peak and 213 at the July 2024 election. The government stated that in one year the number of people housed fell to 16,000 from a previous-government peak of 56,000 (a reported 71% drop), and cited an overall asylum population decline of 13,800 people (-13%) versus last year. Border Security and Asylum Minister Anna Turley attributed the changes to reforms restoring "fairness and control," claiming that small boat arrivals and asylum claims are down while processing and removals are up; these causal links are government assertions rather than independently verified facts.
items.title: UK Home Office reports eight more asylum hotels closed and falling occupancy figures

items.summary: Shen Xiaomeng, director of the UN University Institute for Environment and Human Security (UNU-EHS), told Anadolu Agency at COP31 in Antalya that societies are not lacking scientific knowledge but rather the ability to distill it into messages that reach people's brains and hearts. She argued governments and scientists must improve how findings are communicated so communities can prepare for climate disasters, urging creative approaches such as music and art alongside clearer early warnings. Shen attributed warning-system failures partly to insufficient political willingness to invest in prevention, noting she heard that preventing a disaster costs roughly 5% of its occurrence cost but politicians find long-term gains hard to justify; this figure is her reported characterization rather than an established statistic. She cited deadly German flooding as evidence even developed countries struggle when people cannot interpret technical warning data like water levels. Shen emphasized translating jargon into relatable examples, suggesting burned forest area expressed in football pitches could create emotional connection with audiences. Effective communication depends on public trust in science as a reliable resource for heeding warnings and following guidance. She also called for long-term planning that accounts for interconnected risks with cascading effects, citing Cyclone Amphan during the COVID-19 pandemic when evacuees faced infection risk at shelters; she acknowledged government progress but urged moving beyond short-term responses toward greater adaptation innovation and knowledge sharing between countries. On commitments, Shen said COP31 focused on implementation rather than more pledges, noting some developing nations showed greater ambition than developed ones while securing financial support remained a major challenge, and that post-COP action is the true measure of success.
items.title: UNU-EHS director calls for better climate communication and stronger public trust in science

items.summary: A Spanish police report on a mass migrant crossing at Tarajal beach in Ceuta, which occurred over 30-31 July, estimates that between 8,000 and 10,000 identical black inflatable rings with a printed design were used. Officers say it is not plausible migrants bought thousands of units directly from shops or online on the same day without prior planning, so they believe one large batch was purchased in advance and distributed at specific points before wide use during the crossing; this suggests possible logistical preparation ahead of the arrival. The report notes that social media and press images do not clearly identify sales locations, though some interviewed migrants said they bought rings in the Moroccan town of Fnideq while others acquired them on Tarajal beach itself. Judge María Tardón, handling the case at the National Court, has requested information from the Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in Tarifa about rescues carried out during 30-31 July, including times, locations, identities and units involved, and asked Hazte Oír to provide images of a Ford Focus with a Spanish number plate seen parked on the breakwater before dawn on 30 July. The complaint alleges its occupants assisted only some people crossing; these are allegations in an ongoing case rather than established facts.
items.title: Spanish police report suggests pre-planned migrant ring supply at Ceuta crossing

items.summary: A Russian bombardment of Kyiv on Thursday 19 November 2026 damaged both the Austrian and Dutch embassies, leaving shattered windows, wrecked cars and a blast crater. Ukrainian authorities said Russia fired anti-ship missiles and 98 drones across the country, logging strikes in 18 locations and damaging several diplomatic premises and historic sites; staff at both missions escaped without injury. Deputy head of mission Daniel Ruethlin reported that around 10 people were working inside the Austrian embassy when an explosion occurred during office hours, while Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen said a projectile struck the nearby Dutch embassy with no casualties there either. The Dutch mission was hit two days after weapons manufacturer Destinus revealed Ukraine had used its arms in recent attacks on the Crimean Bridge, prompting Russia's embassy in the Netherlands to accuse The Hague of openly participating in the war; however, no evidence has been provided linking the embassy strikes to that announcement.
items.title: Russian strikes damage Austrian and Dutch embassies in Kyiv

items.summary: US envoy Jared Kushner stated on Thursday that President Donald Trump was open to offering Ukraine a security guarantee resembling NATO's collective-defense provision, while emphasizing Washington must also protect its own interests. The remarks were made during the period surrounding a summit between the presidents of the United States, Russia and China, which German Chancellor Friedrich Merz characterized as merely a 'photo op.'
items.title: Kushner says Trump open to extending NATO-style mutual defense clause to Ukraine

items.summary: María Fernanda Espinosa, described as a UN Secretary-General candidate and former UN General Assembly President, appeared on Euronews' Evening Show Europe Tonight to discuss the latest COP31 climate conference negotiations. The text reports that negotiators from more than 200 countries are racing toward a deal before Friday's deadline, with tensions emerging over climate financing and fossil fuel phase-out—though these claims originate from the program rather than being independently verified. No figures or data beyond the country count were provided.
items.title: Euronews' Europe Tonight debriefs COP31 talks with former UN General Assembly President María Fernanda Espinosa

items.summary: At the APEC CEO Summit 2026, China called for stronger innovation partnerships, deeper cooperation in the digital economy and AI, and a green low-carbon transition to drive growth across the Asia-Pacific. CGTN host Wang Guan moderated a panel with six business leaders from China, the US, Australia and Thailand on advancing these transitions; participants drew on global supply chain experience to discuss how they can boost efficiency, unlock new growth opportunities, and contribute to global sustainable development.
items.title: CGTN panel on digital and green transition drivers of APEC growth

items.summary: In Mahera Beach, Port Loko district, fishers report plastic waste increasingly entangling their nets and forcing costly repairs that halt fishing. Fisher Sheriff Kamara says a recent net tear cost 80 leones (about $3.50) to repair after two days of halted activity; a typical trip uses about 20 liters (5.3 gallons) of petrol costing around 800 leones ($34.70). Fish sellers in the community also bear added costs, with Isatu Jalloh spending between 80 and 90 leones [$3.47-$3.90] on ice blocks and firewood at 50-60 leones [$2.17-$2.60], while delayed returns push up fish prices for buyers. A 2024 study by Lavelle, Preston-Whyte, Lamin, Sankoh, Timbo and Maes recorded 72,901 pieces of litter weighing 1,246 kilograms (2,746 pounds) across Bailor, Tintafor, Kent and Chepo beaches over 11 months, with plastics making up about 70% of items. The World Bank-supported PROBLUE program recovered 48 metric tons of plastic at Mahera within three months, sold to a local recycler supporting more than 30 households mostly women-led; the Ministry's beach-cleaning initiative there has ended. Officials cite Sierra Leone generating an estimated 130,000 metric tons of plastic annually with over half entering the environment, and tourism alone consuming about 42 million single-use plastics yearly with only 6% recycled.
items.title: Plastic pollution undermines fishing livelihoods in coastal Sierra Leone

items.summary: South American media reports say Peruvian authorities raised their count of seized tarantulas in a recent trafficking case from an initial figure to more than 12,000. The final number cited was 12,796 spiders, reportedly announced by the Peruvian National Police (PNP). On Nov. 4, 2026, the Peruvian National Forest and Wildlife Service (SERFOR) said it seized thousands of tarantulas at Jorge Chávez International Airport in Lima, hidden inside socks and plastic containers in luggage bound for Germany; two German citizens and a Polish national were arrested and detained pending further investigation. The spiders spanned life stages from eggs to adults and reportedly originated across Peru, including blue bird eaters (Thrixopelma lagunas), Bolivian blue leg bird eater (Pamphobeteus antinous), other Pamphobeteus species, and several newly described species. Authorities said the alleged traffickers collected them from the wild to sell as exotic pets or for research, valuing the lot at more than half a million euros (around $548,000) on the international market; none of the seized species are protected under CITES but all are protected nationally in Peru. On a TV program, PNP General José Manuel Cruz Chamba reportedly named one arrested individual as Auer Hans Werner, a German national previously detained in 2021 for trafficking nine tarantulas and an egg from Colombia, who is listed among traders at the upcoming Terraristika Hamm fair in Germany; he said traffickers may face 11-20 years if convicted. Sandra Altherr of Pro Wildlife told Mongabay that smugglers keep operating because penalties are too light and small fines make smuggling worthwhile, adding there is hope a longer sentence could be imposed. The case remains under investigation.
items.title: Peru raises its wildlife-trafficking seizure tally to 12,796 tarantulas

items.summary: The Iraqi government under Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi demanded that Iran-allied militia Kataib Hezbollah leave the area of Jurf al-Sakhar by Nov. 20, after an early November report claimed the group had smuggled hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of state-owned oil since 2021; Kataib Hezbollah rejected the ultimatum and said it would not withdraw 'not even over our dead bodies.' The standoff was described as one of the most consequential confrontations between Iraq's government and Iranian-backed militias in more than two decades, though a Reuters report citing three anonymous officials said all parties had agreed to allow government forces into the area on Friday. Analysts note that Kataib Hezbollah is politically embedded: its party Harakat Huqooq belongs to the Coalition Framework bloc that nominated al-Zaidi as prime minister, and some senior members reportedly favor handing territory over to other PMF brigades rather than state security forces. If one militia faction simply replaces another while retaining autonomy, observers say Zaidi would have redistributed armed influence without fundamentally resolving control of the area's oil infrastructure and displaced Sunni residents.
items.title: Iraqi government and Kataib Hezbollah reach a reported compromise over Jurf al-Sakhar

items.summary: Documents released under a provision of the Export Control Reform Act show that, as of May 11, approvals had been cleared through 21 licence applications for Nvidia's H200 chips and their AMD equivalents destined for China. Tencent received approval for 150,000 chips; Alibaba for 75,000; Baidu for 43,000; and BYD for 4,000. All four recipients appear on the defense department's list of alleged Chinese military companies operating in the US. Rep. Brian Mast, chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, used his authority to disclose the licence application details. The disclosures drew criticism from ranking member Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), who said the administration had mishandled export controls and risked national security and the technology edge, questioned enforcement by the Bureau of Industry and Security, and called for rigorous congressional oversight. Nvidia stated that its licensing review spanned more than half a year with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes, and clarified that receiving licences did not mean shipments were continuing, noting it had stopped shipping H200s to China. AMD said it complies with applicable US export control laws and maintains rigorous compliance processes. The disclosure follows earlier scrutiny of the administration's approval of Nvidia's H200 chip sales last year, which Mast investigated; former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang argued that selling China its third- or fourth-best chips would make the country dependent on US-made infrastructure.
items.title: US approved shipments of Nvidia and AMD AI chips to Chinese firms flagged by defense department

items.summary: Dario Amodei, 43, led Anthropic to an IPO on Thursday in New York that raised a record $81 billion and valued the company at about $1.5 trillion; shares debuted at $111.50, 34% above the $83 offering price. At the Nasdaq he said "We will not bend to either business nor political pressure," framing the listing as strengthening resolve to do the right thing. Amodei has emphasized AI safety throughout his rise: in a nearly 4,000-word September essay he warned that AI could outpace human control and urged slowing development while denying any contradiction between safe AI and building powerful models, writing "Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits...while building it too fast is reckless." He quit OpenAI over safety differences. The approach drew criticism from both greater-safety advocates and pro-innovation executives such as Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang, and led to a showdown with the Trump administration in which Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth set a deadline for Anthropic to accept military contract terms that the company rejected, resulting in a government blacklist challenged in court. Amodei said last month the company had "likely sacrificed a significant chunk of a several-month model lead" by delaying its Mythos models over hacking risks and initially limiting access to cybersecurity defenders; an IPO filing noted it paused training of a next-generation flagship model for more than a month over security concerns, while also flagging that its corporate setup could produce decisions conflicting with financial interests. The article attributes the safety emphasis as influencing his management style: Daniela Amodei oversees day-to-day operations while Dario devotes almost 40% of his time to essays and fortnightly "Dario Vision Quests" meetings; a former employee said operationally the buck stops with Daniela, strategically with Dario. The article presents these safety claims as Amodei's stated positions rather than established outcomes, noting that critics dispute whether slowing development serves shareholders.
items.title: Anthropic's Amodei takes his safety approach public

items.summary: All three major US indexes dropped on Thursday, with the S&P 500 down 147.80 points (2.02%) to 7,175.83 after its sixth straight losing session and steepest weekly decline since April 2025; the Dow fell 1,101.11 points (2.19%) to 49,097.06 and the Nasdaq lost 550.68 points (2.25%) to 23,879.20. Anthropic's debut was priced at $83 per share; its shares opened at $111.50, rose as high as $115 (38.6% above the offer price), then pared gains to a 17.1% gain by session close after briefly surpassing a $2 trillion market valuation. Jed Ellerbroek of Argent Capital said money was being pulled from other holdings regardless of direction and that his view on data center capex spending had weakened, citing Nvidia's situation and the midterms; he did not attribute today's decline to the IPO specifically. AMD fell 7.7% after Hunterbrook reported a short position in its affiliated fund Hunterbrook Capital; Micron and Broadcom each dropped 2.1%; Nvidia declined 3.3%, its sixth straight losing session despite an upbeat revenue forecast; CoreWeave fell 6.1% and Nebius slid 9.4%. Palo Alto Networks rose 6.4% after raising 2027 revenue guidance, while Walmart slipped 1.0% on a weak sales forecast. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index closed 2.4% lower and the technology sector ended down 1.9%. Markets are pricing in a 96.4% likelihood of a 25-basis-point rate hike at December's Fed meeting per CME's FedWatch tool, following minutes suggesting a desire to curb inflation ahead of price indexes; next week's PCE report is expected to show year-on-year core inflation of 3.2%, above the central bank's 2% target. On the NYSE declining issues outnumbered advancers by 4.37-to-1 with 21 new highs and 796 new lows, while on Nasdaq declines led advances by 3.55-to-1; volume reached 20.83 billion shares versus a 19.00 billion average over the prior 20 sessions.
items.title: US stocks fell at least 2% as Anthropic's IPO momentum faded

items.summary: Anthropic PBC priced its debut public offering above range and raised $107.3 billion, the largest on record when combining an $81.3 billion primary sale with a $26 billion concurrent private placement that topped SpaceX's June listing; shares closed Thursday at $97.17, up 17% from the $83 IPO price, implying roughly $1.8 trillion in fully diluted value and placing it among the world's ten largest companies by market cap. Demand approached seven times the shares offered, though more than half of bidding institutional investors received no allocation while retail got about 15%. The listing occurred amid a cautious AI trade as the S&P 500 fell 2% and the Nasdaq 100 dropped 2.2%, with analysts citing concerns over Nvidia's role after Jensen Huang's ouster, Democratic midterm gains favoring safety regulation, and worries that financing for heavy users may inflate valuations; one advisor called Anthropic "the most transparent real-time signal of the AI risk trade." The company reported $81 billion in run-rate revenue as of Oct. 31, up about $10 billion from September, with more than 11,900 enterprise customers versus roughly 1,500 a year earlier; it posted a $567 million third-quarter operating loss driven by $5 billion in computing costs and $2 billion in non-cash charges. Goldman Sachs analysts project positive free cash flow only around 2030 against modeled revenue near $685 billion that year, while Bloomberg Intelligence sees value in recursive self-improvement for compute savings and expansion into drug discovery; the stock trades on Nasdaq under ANT with up to 315 million shares available from insiders on day one. No table is included.
items.title: Anthropic's record $107.3 billion IPO values it at roughly $1.8 trillion

items.summary: Anthropic opened trading Thursday and closed its debut up 17% at $97.17 per share after setting an initial offer price of $82 that exceeded the earlier $70 to $78 range, making it the largest IPO in history by overtaking SpaceX's offering. The company offered 980 million shares publicly; at a $83 reference price this translated into about $81 billion from public investors, with an additional $26 billion raised in a concurrent private sale for a total of $107 billion. Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co. attributed the strong debut to investor demand following Nvidia's leadership turmoil over its alleged Chinese spying scandal. CEO Dario Amodei framed safety and profitability as compatible, warning that unchecked AI development could enable autonomous agents to take over the internet within months while citing medical applications like accelerating research into diseases such as plague, smallpox and polio. The IPO came amid concerns about an AI bubble fueled by losses across Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX's AI division; a possible Democratic-led regulatory crackdown on data centers in states including Texas and Georgia; and heavy leverage, with the company carrying $6.2 billion of debt it calls substantial while remaining unprofitable under standard accounting rules despite ample cash that its spending plans could deplete quickly. Amodei cited infrastructure commitments requiring about $900 billion over coming years, including roughly $70 billion in the next 12 months. Rich Lesser of Boston Consulting Group characterized AI market valuations as volatile but more likely to rise than fall over many years while calling the industry's progress remarkable.
items.title: Anthropic's record IPO closed up 17% at $97.17, raising a total of $107 billion

items.summary: The US International Trade Commission's Export Enforcement Committee, chaired by Republican Brian Mast, said he exercised his authorities under the Export Control Reform Act to publicly reveal information about NVIDIA and AMD AI chip export control licenses for China. The committee reported requested sales of 3.4 million AI chips to China against approval of more than 879,000 by BIS, including approvals covering exports to Chinese military companies designated by the Department of War such as Alibaba and Tencent. It also alleges requests by NVIDIA to use possible chip-smuggling fronts to facilitate advanced AI chip sales to Chinese companies. These figures are reported findings from a committee statement rather than independently verified data.
items.title: US House committee chairman disclosed NVIDIA and AMD export license applications for China

items.summary: The House Foreign Affairs Committee reported that the Trump administration licensed exports of 879,000 advanced AI chips from Nvidia and AMD to Chinese firms between December 2025 and May 2026. The Department of Commerce approvals covered Alibaba (75,000), Tencent (150,000), Baidu (43,000) and BYD (4,000). Companies had sought permission to ship 3.4 million chips during the period; it was unclear how many licenses resulted in actual shipments. All four companies appear on the Pentagon's list of alleged Chinese military-backed firms. Committee chair Brian Mast invoked Export Control Reform Act authority to release the data amid scrutiny following revelations about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and renewed pressure for a tougher stance against China tech threats. Chris McGuire, a former US official, said over 30 percent of AI chips sent to China went to companies designated by the Department of War as military-linked, questioning whether Commerce conducted serious national security review; this is an assertion attributed to him rather than established fact. Nvidia stated its approvals were subject to strict conditions and limited volumes, that it had stopped shipping H200s to China since receiving some licenses, and that AMD did not immediately comment. Nvidia's stock fell 3.3 percent while AMD dropped 7.7 percent; the Nasdaq and S&P 500 declined 2.2 percent and 1.8 percent respectively.
items.title: US approved nearly 900,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chips for China in six months

items.summary: A Supreme Court bench of CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana ruled that in housing projects left incomplete despite banks disbursing most loan instalments to builders who became insolvent or rogue, commercial courts, NCLT or NCLAT cannot require flat buyers to repay the lender without first examining what the bench called the "unholy" bank-builder nexus. The order arose from a petition by homebuyers in Raheja Developers' Krishna housing project in Gurgaon, which has entered insolvency proceedings; those buyers said banks began recovery in a Saket commercial court even though they had not received their flats. The bench held that it is the bounden duty of the commercial court to determine whether the bank disbursed funds strictly per the tripartite agreement and issued an interim direction that no coercive action be taken against similarly placed homebuyers unless a categorical finding establishes buyer default, since under such agreements loans were meant to flow directly to builders in proportion to construction progress. The bench noted that builder-bank collusion often caused lenders to release far more than the amount warranted by the stage of construction, and that recovery suits threatened buyers who had paid EMIs while never receiving flats; it added that a Sept order directing CBI inquiries into collusive misuse of the subvention scheme underpins this reasoning. The bench also warned that its sympathy for homebuyers has opened "the floodgates of litigation," with thousands rushing to the Supreme Court, and said its hands are full and it may not handle fresh cases; in a separate Bengaluru case involving over 4,000 buyers who had paid about 95% of their flat's cost despite nearly a decade of incomplete construction, it granted protection but directed counsel to seek relief from the Karnataka High Court. The ruling is an interim direction on this specific petition and does not establish that all such recovery suits must fail.
items.title: Supreme Court bars commercial courts from recovering home loans without first examining builder-bank nexus

items.summary: The UNFPA State of the World Population Report 2026, released Thursday, places India as the world's most populous country with an estimated 1.47 billion people (147.66 crore) for 2026, a population doubling time of 81 years, and growth projected to about 1.7 billion before declining roughly four decades hence. The report attributes India's status as the world's largest nation to surpassing China in 2023 (India at 142.86 crore versus China at 142.57 crore). It frames a large share of young people aged 10-24, accounting for about 26% of the population, as India's 'youth moment' and calls for investing while that dividend window remains open. The report flags India's total fertility rate at 1.9, below the replacement level of 2.1 births per woman, though it does not attribute this decline to a specific cause. It also reports life expectancy figures (71 years for males, 74 for females), demographic breakdowns across age brackets, and draws on UNFPA's global Demographic Futures Survey of more than 108,000 internet-connected adults in 73 countries including 1,722 from India.
